newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine wheat farmers want new quality stamps.
newsitem.headline: Argentine wheat farmers want new quality stamps.

text.p: Argentine wheat could be marketed according to a new system of classifications designed to guarantee quality and maximize prices by as early as next harvest, an official of a new farmers' association said Monday.

"Our raison d'etre is to promote actions which will lead to an increase in the value of the crop," Sean Cameron, secretary of the Argentine Wheat Producers Association, told Reuters from his property in the southern Buenos Aires province wheat belt.

The farmers want to replace Argentina's present system of classifying wheat according to just three qualities with a more complicated system of grades according to milling properties such as protein level and specific weight.

Argentine wheat is presently jumbled into storage and ships with little regard for differences of quality, putting the country at a marketing disadvantage compared to slicker competitors such as Canada.

"If a Brazilian miller comes along and says we want 20,000 tonnes of wheat a month with a minimum 12 percent protein level, then we can't sell to that guy on those terms," Cameron said, "Even though we've got the wheat."
Formed late last year, the association sent a delegation to meet the government's farm chief, Agriculture Secretary Felipe Sola, last week to propose a new system of classifying wheat.
"We met the secretary, who would like it to be done more quickly," Cameron said. "They see it partly on course for this coming crop. We did not imagine it that quick."

He added the shared objective of the association and the government is to quickly introduce a new scale of quality and certificates of quality at origin and then appoint a policing body to make sure it is upheld. Sola said he wanted the revised quality grades to be ready before the 1997/98 harvest.
But the association has no ambitions to rival the Canadian Wheat Board, a government body which buys and markets all of Canada's wheat.

"We don't aim to do that, we won't be a selling agency as such, but rather to try and do things which increase the price we eventually receive," Cameron said, "The crux is differentiating and storing by quality."

With about 50 million tonnes of installed grain storage capacity for an annual wheat crop of 15 million tonnes, Argentina already has most of the infrastructure it needs to separate its wheat into different qualities for marketing.
"It doesn't need a great building effort or anything, but more in change in attitude," Cameron said, "It should be logistically possible."
While it has government suppport, the fledgling association still has few members among farmers and still has to woo exporters over.
"I think they'll eventually realize it's the way we have got to go," Cameron said.
Ironically, he said, the arch-competitors at the Canadian Wheat Board have expressed support for the Argentine farmers' initiative.

"The way things are now, world wheat prices drop if a big Argentine crop is looming, as its quality is of a lower common denominator," Cameron said, "It is in their (the Canadians') interests if we can better sell our crop."
